title: Declaration Files and @types
summary: A declaration file describes the types of code that is written somewhere else.
introduction: A declaration file describes the types of code that is written somewhere else. Think of a menu that tells you what you can order. The menu does not cook the food. In the same way, this file describes code but does not run it.
learningObjectives: Explain what a .d.ts file contains and generate one with the declaration option
Fix TS7016 by installing @types packages or writing a declare module block
Augment global types such as process.env with declare global

blocks.text: A `.d.ts` file is the type-level half of a module: the signatures of its exports with the bodies removed. The compiler produces them for your own code when `"declaration": true` is set, and that is what library authors publish next to their JavaScript so consumers get types without the source. Compile this file and look at the result.

blocks.title: src/geometry.ts
npx tsc --declaration, then cat dist/geometry.d.ts

blocks.text: The `declare` keyword means *this exists, but its implementation lives elsewhere*. `dist/geometry.js` holds the implementation; `dist/geometry.d.ts` lets another project type-check calls to `distance` without reading the JavaScript. The built-in `lib.*.d.ts` files that ship with TypeScript describe the JavaScript language and the DOM in exactly this way, which is how the compiler knows that `Math.hypot` returns a number.

Most popular packages now ship their own `.d.ts` files, listed in the `types` or `exports` field of their `package.json`. Packages written in plain JavaScript rely on the community-maintained DefinitelyTyped repository, published as `@types/<name>`: `@types/node` for Node's APIs, `@types/express`, `@types/lodash` and thousands more. When neither exists, importing the package produces TS7016.

blocks.title: src/use-untyped.ts (legacy-slugify is an imaginary JavaScript-only package)
npx tsc (path shortened)
blocks.content:
src/use-untyped.ts:1:21 - error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module 'legacy-slugify'. '.../node_modules/legacy-slugify/index.js' implicitly has an 'any' type.
  Try `npm i --save-dev @types/legacy-slugify` if it exists or add a new declaration (.d.ts) file containing `declare module 'legacy-slugify';`

1 import slugify from "legacy-slugify";
                      ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in src/use-untyped.ts:1

blocks.text: The message lists the fixes in order of preference. First try `npm install --save-dev @types/legacy-slugify`; if the package exists, the error disappears with no further work. If it does not, write the declaration yourself.

Create a `.d.ts` file inside the project (a `types` folder is conventional) and describe the parts of the package you use. The file must be visible to the compiler: add the folder to `include` in `tsconfig.json`. Everything inside `declare module "name"` is an ambient declaration, so there are no bodies, only signatures.

blocks.title: types/legacy-slugify.d.ts
npx tsc && node dist/use-untyped.js (after adding "types" to include)
Common mistake: the one-line shorthand
blocks.text: The error message also offers `declare module 'legacy-slugify';` with no body. That shorthand types every export of the package as `any`, so the import compiles but calls are unchecked: `slugify(42)` or `slugify()` would pass. Use it only as a temporary measure while migrating, and prefer a real declaration of the functions you call, even if it covers only a fraction of the package.

`@types/node` declares `process.env` as a dictionary of `string | undefined`, which is correct in general but inconvenient for variables your deployment guarantees. A `declare global` block inside a module file (the `export {}` makes it one) merges extra members into the existing `ProcessEnv` interface, thanks to the declaration merging that interfaces support.

blocks.title: src/env.d.ts
src/env-use.ts
npx tsc
blocks.content:
src/env-use.ts:3:7 - error TS2322: Type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.

3 const region: string = process.env.REGION;
        ~~~~~~


Found 1 error in src/env-use.ts:3

blocks.text: `DATABASE_URL` is now a plain `string` and `PORT` is `string | undefined`, exactly as declared, while the undeclared `REGION` keeps the cautious default and is rejected. Remember that the declaration is a promise: the program must still refuse to start when `DATABASE_URL` is really missing. The same `declare global` technique adds properties to `Window` in browser code, and a bare `declare const __BUILD_ID__: string;` declares a global that a bundler injects at build time.

rows: Emit a `.d.ts` next to every `.js`; required for publishing a typed library
Lets *Go to definition* jump from a `.d.ts` to the original `.ts` source
Include only the listed `@types` packages instead of every one in `node_modules/@types` (the 5.9 `tsc --init` template sets `types: []`)
Do not type-check `.d.ts` files; faster builds and immunity to conflicts between packages, at the cost of not checking your own `.d.ts` files
Which built-in declaration files to load; drop `dom` for pure Node code

blocks.title: Checking what the compiler sees
blocks.text: `npx tsc --listFiles` prints every file in the program, including the `.d.ts` files it loaded, and `--explainFiles` says why each one was included. Both are the fastest way to find out why a global is unknown or why two copies of a type conflict.

questions.question: A `.d.ts` file can contain function bodies that run at runtime.
questions.explanation: Declaration files hold only types and ambient declarations. They produce no JavaScript and cannot contain implementations.

questions.question: Why does `src/env.d.ts` start with `export {};`?
questions.explanation: A file with no import or export is a global script. The empty export turns it into a module, which is required for declare global to be allowed and keeps its other declarations out of the global scope.
options: To export the ProcessEnv interface for other files
To make the file a module so that `declare global` is permitted
Because every .d.ts file must export something
To prevent the compiler from emitting JavaScript for it
